You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems

*(Text as amended by the manager's amendment of Oct. 6, 2026)*

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-metric-ton limit applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could split recovery across several vessels, each below the threshold, and mine any total amount legally. Nothing aggregates tonnage by operator, company, or project.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "per year" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether "year" means a calendar year, the operator's fiscal year, or any rolling 12 months. It also doesn't say whether tonnage is measured wet (as lifted, including water and sediment) or dry, which could change the total substantially.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "recovery" undefined.** It's unclear whether recovery means lifting material to the surface, collecting it on the seabed, or landing it at port. An operator could argue that collecting or stockpiling nodules on the seafloor is not "recovery."

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "other mineral resources" undefined.** The phrase could be read to include sand, gravel, or even hydrocarbons, or it could be read narrowly. Without a definition or a cross-reference (e.g., to DSHMRA, 30 U.S.C. 1403), its scope is open to argument in both directions.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A): no geographic scope.** The definition covers any seabed deeper than 200 meters but doesn't say whether that means the U.S. EEZ and continental shelf, the international seabed Area, or other nations' waters. Read with Sec. 3(a), this leaves the bill's reach unclear.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "Secretary" is never defined.** Neither Sec. 2 nor any other section says which Secretary (Commerce? Interior?) makes the determination. As written, (B) arguably cannot be implemented at all.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B): vague standard and no procedure.** "Risks … comparable to" the activities in (A) has no criteria, no rulemaking or notice-and-comment requirement, and no review process. Because violations carry criminal penalties (Sec. 5(b)), this invites void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges, and agency interpretations no longer receive Chevron deference after *Loper Bright* (2024).

8. **Sec. 2(2): narrow "U.S. person" definition.** The definition covers only citizens and *corporations*. LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entity types fall outside it, as do lawful permanent residents and foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies. A U.S. firm could operate through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary or a non-corporate entity.

9. **Sec. 2(2): "State" undefined.** It's unclear whether entities organized under the laws of D.C., Puerto Rico, or other territories, or under federal charter, count as U.S. persons.

10. **Sec. 2(3): covered-vessel definition is disconnected from the prohibition.** The prohibition (Sec. 2(1)(A)) applies to any vessel, but registration (Sec. 4) applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons. Smaller vessels can mine without registering, and fleets of small vessels avoid both the tonnage threshold and the registry.

11. **Sec. 2(3): "equipped for the recovery" is easy to avoid.** An operator could remove or swap equipment between voyages, or classify the gear as research or survey equipment, to stay outside the definition.

## Prohibition (Sec. 3)

12. **Sec. 3(a): "United States" undefined geographically.** It's unclear whether "in the United States" includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. A foreign company mining in the U.S. EEZ from a foreign-flagged vessel could argue it is not covered.

13. **Sec. 3(a): "person" undefined.** The bill defines "U.S. person" but not "person," so it's unclear which entities are covered under the "any person in the United States" prong.

14. **Sec. 3(a): only direct mining is prohibited.** The bill doesn't prohibit financing, sponsoring, contracting for, aiding, or directing mining, or importing, purchasing, processing, or selling seabed minerals. U.S. companies could fund foreign operators and buy their output, and foreign-mined nodules could be processed in the U.S.

15. **Sec. 3(b): the grandfather clause is open-ended.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license issued before … enactment" with no expiration, no tonnage cap, and no limits on renewal, transfer, or expansion. A pre-enactment license could cover large-scale operations indefinitely, up to the Sec. 7(b) sunset.

16. **Sec. 3(b): mismatch between "exploration" and "mining."** Under DSHMRA, exploration licenses don't authorize commercial recovery; that requires a separate commercial recovery permit. As drafted, the clause could be read either to grandfather commercial-scale mining under mere exploration licenses, or to grandfather nothing meaningful. Meanwhile, holders of commercial recovery permits are oddly *not* grandfathered.

17. **Sec. 3(b): no issuing authority specified.** "An exploration license" isn't limited to licenses issued by NOAA under DSHMRA. Licenses or contracts from the International Seabed Authority or a foreign sponsoring state could arguably qualify.

18. **Sec. 3(b): incentive to rush licenses before enactment.** Because the cutoff is enactment, companies have an incentive to obtain exploration licenses while the bill is pending. Nothing in the bill freezes new licensing during that period.

19. **Sec. 3(c): environmental-assessment exemption is self-certifying.** The exemption turns on the "purpose" of the activity, with no definition, permit, tonnage cap, duration limit, or oversight. Commercial-scale recovery could be relabeled as assessment, and nothing bars selling material recovered under the exemption.

20. **Sec. 3 generally: no relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), which still directs NOAA to issue licenses and permits. That creates a statutory conflict that courts would have to resolve, and that companies could exploit.

## Registry (Sec. 4)

21. **Sec. 4: no penalty for failing to register or report.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register, not filing reports, or filing inaccurate reports carries no penalty under the Act. The general false-statements statute, 18 U.S.C. 1001, might reach knowingly false certified reports, but nothing addresses simple non-filing.

22. **Sec. 4(a): no deadline or scope.** Registration has no deadline, no required information, and no stated geographic or nationality scope. It's unclear whether it applies to foreign operators of foreign vessels outside U.S. waters, and "operator" is undefined.

23. **Sec. 4(b): reports don't have to include tonnage.** Reports must "describe recovery activities" but aren't required to include tonnage, location, or depth, which are exactly the facts needed to determine whether the Sec. 2(1)(A) threshold has been crossed.

24. **Sec. 4: no monitoring or inspection authority.** The bill provides no vessel tracking, observers, boarding or inspection rights, subpoena power, or recordkeeping requirements. Enforcement would rely almost entirely on operators' self-reporting.

## Penalties and Enforcement (Sec. 5)

25. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8: effective-date conflict.** Sec. 5(a) imposes penalties for violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days after enactment. This creates ambiguity, and a likely fair-notice challenge, over whether conduct during that window is punishable.

26. **Sec. 5(a): unclear how to count "days of violation."** A violation of Sec. 2(1)(A) depends on an annual total, so it's unclear which days count. Is it only the days after the 10,000-ton mark is crossed, or every mining day that year? That ambiguity affects penalty exposure by orders of magnitude.

27. **Sec. 5: no enforcing agency or procedure.** The bill doesn't say who assesses civil penalties, whether they are imposed administratively or in court, or what hearing rights apply. After *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024), civil penalties imposed administratively may face Seventh Amendment jury-trial challenges.

28. **Sec. 5: limited remedies.** There's no injunctive relief authority, no forfeiture of vessels or recovered minerals, no citizen-suit provision, and no whistleblower provision. Penalties alone may be a weak deterrent if recovered minerals are worth more than the fines.

29. **Sec. 5(b): criminal liability tied to a vague definition.** Willful violations carry up to 10 years in prison, but the conduct includes whatever the undefined Secretary designates under Sec. 2(1)(B). That makes criminal prosecutions under (B) especially vulnerable to vagueness challenges.

## International Agreement (Sec. 6)

30. **Sec. 6: ambiguous and unenforceable.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" could mean begin seeking within 18 months or conclude within 18 months. There's no reporting requirement and no consequence if nothing happens. It's also unclear how this interacts with the ISA process, given that the U.S. isn't a party to UNCLOS.

## Duration (Sec. 7)

31. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): internal contradiction.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues *until* Congress makes a finding, but (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless of any finding. As a result, operators can simply wait out the prohibition.

32. **Sec. 7(a): no NAS report is actually required.** The finding must be based on a National Academies report, but the bill doesn't commission, fund, or set a deadline for one. "Serious harm" is also undefined.

33. **Sec. 7(a): the mechanism may be legally redundant.** A joint resolution requires presentment to the President, making it effectively a new law. Congress could end the prohibition by statute anyway, so (a) adds little legal effect.

34. **Sec. 7(b): effective term is shorter than it appears, and there's no savings clause.** The sunset runs from enactment, but the Act takes effect 180 days later, so the prohibition actually runs about 9.5 years. There's also no savings clause, so it's uncertain whether penalties for pre-sunset violations could still be enforced after the Act expires. The general savings statute, 1 U.S.C. 109, addresses repeal, and its application to expiration is less settled.

## Effective Date and Missing Provisions

35. **Sec. 8: 180-day window allows lawful stockpiling.** Mining during the 180 days after enactment is lawful, which encourages companies to accelerate recovery and stockpile before the ban begins.

36. **Whole bill: no rulemaking authority.** No agency is authorized to issue implementing regulations, which leaves the definitions, the registry, and the penalty procedures without a way to be filled in.

37. **Whole bill: no severability clause.** If a court strikes down one provision, such as the Sec. 2(1)(B) delegation, there's no clause signaling that Congress intended the rest of the bill to stand.

## Possible Markup Story Angles

Measured by practical effect on whether companies could keep operating, the most consequential items are probably these:

- **#1:** Splitting tonnage across multiple vessels.
- **#8 and #14:** Operating through subsidiaries or non-corporate entities, and the lack of an import/financing ban.
- **#15–16:** The open-ended grandfather clause.
- **#19:** The self-certifying assessment exemption.
- **#21:** No penalty for failing to register or report.
- **#31:** The sunset that overrides the Sec. 7(a) process.

Amendments targeting any of these at Thursday's markup would be worth watching.

**Caveats:**

- This is a textual analysis of the language you pasted. Check it against the official manager's amendment text before publishing.
- Where possible, attribute legal-vulnerability points (especially #7, #27, and #29) to outside legal experts or CRS rather than stating them as our own conclusions.
- Some of these "loopholes" may be deliberate policy choices by the sponsors (e.g., the 200-meter depth floor or the grandfather clause). Asking the committee staff about intent before characterizing them would keep our coverage fair.
